---
title: "Class 18: Manufactured Solutions and Galerkin Orthogonality"
subtitle: "Where the exact solution comes from, and why the estimate describes our answer"
format:
  html:
    page-layout: full
    toc: true
---

The discussion in Class 17 did not cover two important parts of convergence analysis.
First, we spent a whole class measuring how far $u^h$ is from $u$, without ever saying where $u$ is supposed to come from. 
On a real problem we don't actually have $u$, and that is why we running the solver in the first place. 
The second is theoretical: the error estimate we wrote down is a statement about *polynomials*, and we never justified using it to describe the answer our solver actually produced.
Today will cover both of these issues.

## Manufacturing a solution

### Running the problem backwards

Normally you are handed $f$, $\mathcal{g}$ and $\mathcal{h}$, and you go looking for $u$.
That is the hard direction, and in general there is no formula at the end of it.

The trick is to run the arrow the other way. **Pick the answer first, then work out which
problem it solves.** Choosing $u$ is free --- you can write down any function you like --- and
once you have it, finding the data that produces it is just differentiation, which is easy.

For the problem we have been solving all semester,

$$
u_{,xx} + f = 0 \ \text{ on } \Omega = (0,L), \qquad
u(L) = \mathcal{g}, \qquad -u_{,x}(0) = \mathcal{h},
$$

the recipe is three steps:

1. **Choose** any $u$ you like, as long as it is smooth enough to differentiate twice.
2. **Differentiate** it twice and set $f = -u_{,xx}$.
3. **Evaluate** at the two ends: $\mathcal{g} = u(L)$ and $\mathcal{h} = -u_{,x}(0)$.

Now feed $f$, $\mathcal{g}$ and $\mathcal{h}$ to your solver. It has no idea anything unusual
has happened --- it is solving an ordinary boundary value problem. But *you* know the exact
answer, so you can subtract it from $u^h$ and measure the error for real.

This is called a **manufactured solution**, and it is how essentially all finite element
software is verified.

### A worked example

Take

$$ u(x) = \sin(\pi x) \qquad \text{on } \Omega = (0,1) . $$

Differentiate twice:

$$ u_{,x} = \pi \cos(\pi x), \qquad u_{,xx} = -\pi^2 \sin(\pi x), $$

so the forcing that produces this solution is

$$ f = -u_{,xx} = \pi^2 \sin(\pi x) . $$

The boundary data comes straight from evaluating:

$$ \mathcal{g} = u(1) = \sin(\pi) = 0, \qquad \mathcal{h} = -u_{,x}(0) = -\pi . $$

That is the whole derivation. Hand $f = \pi^2\sin(\pi x)$, $\mathcal{g} = 0$ and
$\mathcal{h} = -\pi$ to the solver, run the convergence study from Class 17, and the
measured rates come out as

| $p$ | $H^0$ rate | $H^1$ rate | predicted |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 2.00 | 1.00 | 2, 1 |
| 2 | 3.00 | 2.00 | 3, 2 |
| 3 | 3.98 | 3.00 | 4, 3 |

exactly the $\beta = p + 1 - s$ the estimate promised.

The picture below is that solve. The left panels are the solution and its derivative; the
convergence plots underneath are the same study run out to 64 elements, with a marker
showing where the current choice of degree and mesh sits.

```{=html}
var PI=Math.PI;
function u(x){ return Math.sin(PI*x); }
function du(x){ return PI*Math.cos(PI*x); }

function nodes(p){ var v=[]; for(var i=0;i<=p;i++) v.push(-1+2*i/p); return v; }
function lag(p,a,xi){ var n=nodes(p),v=1;
  for(var b=0;b<=p;b++) if(b!==a) v*=(xi-n[b])/(n[a]-n[b]);
  return v; }
function dlag(p,a,xi){ var n=nodes(p),s=0;
  for(var c=0;c<=p;c++){ if(c===a) continue;
    var t=1/(n[a]-n[c]);
    for(var b=0;b<=p;b++) if(b!==a&&b!==c) t*=(xi-n[b])/(n[a]-n[b]);
    s+=t; }
  return s; }
function D(){ return COEF[P+'_'+NE]; }
// IEN(p,a,e) = a + p*e, exactly as in the course code
function uhLocal(e,xi,deriv){
  var d=D(), v=0, he=1/NE;
  for(var a=0;a<=P;a++){
    var c=d[a+P*e];
    v += deriv ? c*dlag(P,a,xi)*(2/he) : c*lag(P,a,xi);
  }
  return v; }

function txt(x,y,s,o){ o=o||{};
  var t=el('text',{x:x,y:y,'font-size':o.fs||12,fill:o.fill||GREY,
    'text-anchor':o.ta||'start','font-family':o.ff||'system-ui, sans-serif'});
  if(o.fw) t.setAttribute('font-weight',o.fw);
  t.textContent=s; return t; }

// ---------------- top: solution and derivative ----------------
function panel(g,X0,X1,Y0,Y1,title,deriv){
  var exact = deriv?du:u;
  // sample the exact function and the approximation element by element,
  // so the discontinuities in the derivative are not bridged
  var lo=1e30, hi=-1e30, segs=[], i, e, k, xi, x, ve, va, pts;
  var NS=24;
  for(e=0;e<NE;e++){
    pts=[];
    for(k=0;k<=NS;k++){
      xi=-1+2*k/NS; x=(e+(xi+1)/2)/NE;
      ve=exact(x); va=uhLocal(e,xi,deriv);
      var y = SHOWERR ? (ve-va) : va;
      pts.push([x,y]);
      if(y<lo)lo=y; if(y>hi)hi=y;
      if(!SHOWERR){ if(ve<lo)lo=ve; if(ve>hi)hi=ve; }
    }
    segs.push(pts);
  }
  if(!SHOWERR){ for(k=0;k<=240;k++){ var xx=k/240, vv=exact(xx);
    if(vv<lo)lo=vv; if(vv>hi)hi=vv; } }
  if(hi-lo<1e-14){ hi=lo+1; lo-=0; }
  var pad=(hi-lo)*0.14; lo-=pad; hi+=pad;
  function sx(x){ return X0+x*(X1-X0); }
  function sy(y){ return Y1-(y-lo)/(hi-lo)*(Y1-Y0); }

  g.appendChild(el('rect',{x:X0,y:Y0,width:X1-X0,height:Y1-Y0,fill:'#fff',stroke:FAINT}));
  g.appendChild(txt((X0+X1)/2,Y0-12,title,{ta:'middle',fs:13,fill:INK,fw:600}));
  // element boundaries
  for(e=0;e<=NE;e++){ var xb=sx(e/NE);
    g.appendChild(el('line',{x1:xb,y1:Y0,x2:xb,y2:Y1,stroke:FAINT,'stroke-width':1})); }
  // zero line
  if(lo<0&&hi>0){ g.appendChild(el('line',{x1:X0,y1:sy(0),x2:X1,y2:sy(0),
    stroke:FAINT,'stroke-width':1,'stroke-dasharray':'3 3'})); }
  // approximation (or error), one path per element
  for(i=0;i<segs.length;i++){
    var dd='';
    for(k=0;k<segs[i].length;k++) dd+=(k?'L':'M')+sx(segs[i][k][0]).toFixed(2)+' '+sy(segs[i][k][1]).toFixed(2);
    g.appendChild(el('path',{d:dd,fill:'none',stroke:SHOWERR?ACC:PC[P-1],'stroke-width':2}));
  }
  // exact curve (only when showing values)
  if(!SHOWERR){
    var d='';
    for(k=0;k<=240;k++){ var xv=k/240; d+=(k?'L':'M')+sx(xv).toFixed(2)+' '+sy(exact(xv)).toFixed(2); }
    g.appendChild(el('path',{d:d,fill:'none',stroke:GREY,'stroke-width':1.6,'stroke-dasharray':'5 4'}));
  }
  // nodes
  if(!SHOWERR && !deriv){
    for(e=0;e<NE;e++) for(var a=0;a<=P;a++){
      if(e>0&&a===0) continue;
      var xn=(e+a/P)/NE;
      g.appendChild(el('circle',{cx:sx(xn),cy:sy(D()[a+P*e]),r:2.6,fill:PC[P-1]}));
    }
  }
  // y labels
  g.appendChild(txt(X0-6,Y0+4,hi.toExponential(1),{ta:'end',fs:10}));
  g.appendChild(txt(X0-6,Y1,lo.toExponential(1),{ta:'end',fs:10}));
  g.appendChild(txt(X0,Y1+15,'0',{fs:11}));
  g.appendChild(txt(X1,Y1+15,'1',{ta:'end',fs:11}));
  g.appendChild(txt((X0+X1)/2,Y1+15,'x',{ta:'middle',fs:11}));
}

function drawTop(){
  var s=document.getElementById('w18top'); s.innerHTML='';
  var g=el('g',{}); s.appendChild(g);
  panel(g,56,418,56,330, SHOWERR?'error in the solution':'u = sin(πx) and uʰ', false);
  panel(g,500,862,56,330, SHOWERR?'error in the derivative':'uₒₓ and the derivative of uʰ', true);
  var lg=el('g',{}); s.appendChild(lg);
  if(!SHOWERR){
    lg.appendChild(el('line',{x1:56,y1:368,x2:86,y2:368,stroke:GREY,'stroke-width':1.6,'stroke-dasharray':'5 4'}));
    lg.appendChild(txt(92,372,'exact',{fs:12}));
    lg.appendChild(el('line',{x1:150,y1:368,x2:180,y2:368,stroke:PC[P-1],'stroke-width':2}));
    lg.appendChild(txt(186,372,'finite element solution, p='+P+', '+NE+' elements',{fs:12}));
  } else {
    lg.appendChild(el('line',{x1:56,y1:368,x2:86,y2:368,stroke:ACC,'stroke-width':2}));
    lg.appendChild(txt(92,372,'u − uʰ, drawn one element at a time',{fs:12}));
  }
}

// ---------------- bottom: convergence ----------------
var YMIN=1e-13, YMAX=10;
function cpanel(g,X0,X1,Y0,Y1,key,title){
  function sx(n){ return X0+(Math.log(n)-Math.log(2))/(Math.log(64)-Math.log(2))*(X1-X0); }
  function sy(v){ v=Math.max(v,YMIN);
    return Y1-(Math.log10(v)-Math.log10(YMIN))/(Math.log10(YMAX)-Math.log10(YMIN))*(Y1-Y0); }
  g.appendChild(el('rect',{x:X0,y:Y0,width:X1-X0,height:Y1-Y0,fill:'#fff',stroke:FAINT}));
  g.appendChild(txt((X0+X1)/2,Y0-12,title,{ta:'middle',fs:13,fill:INK,fw:600}));
  var k,p,i;
  for(k=-13;k<=1;k+=3){
    var yy=sy(Math.pow(10,k));
    g.appendChild(el('line',{x1:X0,y1:yy,x2:X1,y2:yy,stroke:FAINT,'stroke-width':1}));
    g.appendChild(txt(X0-5,yy+3,'1e'+k,{ta:'end',fs:9.5}));
  }
  var ticks=[2,4,8,16,32,64];
  for(i=0;i<ticks.length;i++){
    var xx=sx(ticks[i]);
    g.appendChild(el('line',{x1:xx,y1:Y0,x2:xx,y2:Y1,stroke:FAINT,'stroke-width':1}));
    g.appendChild(txt(xx,Y1+14,''+ticks[i],{ta:'middle',fs:10}));
  }
  g.appendChild(txt((X0+X1)/2,Y1+30,'number of elements',{ta:'middle',fs:11}));
  var endy=[];
  for(p=1;p<=5;p++){
    var a=ERR[p][key], d='';
    for(i=0;i<CONV.length;i++) d+=(i?'L':'M')+sx(CONV[i]).toFixed(2)+' '+sy(a[i]).toFixed(2);
    g.appendChild(el('path',{d:d,fill:'none',stroke:PC[p-1],
      'stroke-width':(p===P?2.6:1.2),opacity:(p===P?1:0.42)}));
    endy.push(sy(a[a.length-1]));
  }
  // p=4 and p=5 both bottom out, so their labels would land on top of each other
  for(i=1;i<endy.length;i++) if(endy[i]-endy[i-1]<11) endy[i]=endy[i-1]+11;
  for(p=1;p<=5;p++)
    g.appendChild(txt(sx(64)+4,endy[p-1]+3,'p='+p,{fs:10,fill:PC[p-1]}));
  var j=CONV.indexOf(NE), cv=ERR[P][key][j];
  g.appendChild(el('circle',{cx:sx(NE),cy:sy(cv),r:6.5,fill:'none',stroke:INK,'stroke-width':1.8}));
  g.appendChild(el('circle',{cx:sx(NE),cy:sy(cv),r:2.6,fill:INK}));
}

function drawBot(){
  var s=document.getElementById('w18bot'); s.innerHTML='';
  var g=el('g',{}); s.appendChild(g);
  cpanel(g,56,400,56,330,'L2','error in H⁰ (the L² norm)');
  cpanel(g,500,844,56,330,'H1','error in H¹');
}

function cap(){
  var j=CONV.indexOf(NE);
  var e0=ERR[P]['L2'][j], e1=ERR[P]['H1'][j];
  var k=CONV.indexOf(32), kk=CONV.indexOf(64);
  var r0=Math.log(ERR[P]['L2'][k]/ERR[P]['L2'][kk])/Math.log(2);
  var r1=Math.log(ERR[P]['H1'][k]/ERR[P]['H1'][kk])/Math.log(2);
  var s='<b>p = '+P+', '+NE+' elements.</b> '+
    'Error here is '+e0.toExponential(2)+' in H⁰ and '+e1.toExponential(2)+' in H¹. '+
    'Between 32 and 64 elements the curves above have slope '+r0.toFixed(2)+' and '+r1.toFixed(2)+
    ', against the predicted '+(P+1)+' and '+P+'. ';
  if(P>=4) s+='<b>Notice the H⁰ curve flattening at the bottom right.</b> '+
    'At this degree the error reaches roughly 10⁻¹² after a few refinements, which is as '+
    'small as double precision can represent it. The slope there is telling you about '+
    'arithmetic, not about the method — at p = 5 it even turns upward.';
  else s+='The finite element solution also passes through the exact solution at every node, '+
    'which is special to this one-dimensional problem.';
  document.getElementById('w18cap').innerHTML=s;
}

function draw(){ drawTop(); drawBot(); cap(); }

document.getElementById('w18deg').addEventListener('click',function(ev){
  var b=ev.target.closest('button'); if(!b) return;
  P=+b.dataset.p;
  var bs=this.querySelectorAll('button');
  for(var i=0;i<bs.length;i++) bs[i].setAttribute('aria-pressed', bs[i]===b?'true':'false');
  draw();
});
document.getElementById('w18ne').addEventListener('input',function(){
  NE=+this.value; document.getElementById('w18nev').textContent=NE; draw(); });
document.getElementById('w18err').addEventListener('change',function(){
  SHOWERR=this.checked; draw(); });

draw();
})();
</script>
```

### What this does and does not tell you

A manufactured solution is a **verification** tool: it answers *did I implement the method
correctly?* If your rates come out at the predicted $\beta$, your basis functions, your
Jacobians, your assembly and your boundary conditions are almost certainly all right. It is
a remarkably sharp test --- most coding mistakes break the rate, not just the constant,
because they break the method rather than merely making it less accurate.

What it does **not** tell you is whether you solved the right problem. The physics, the
geometry, the material data and the boundary conditions you chose are all still your
responsibility. Verification asks whether you solved the equations right; it does not ask
whether you had the right equations.

One more caution. You are free to pick any $u$, which means you are also free to pick one
that makes the test easier than it should be. If you choose a $u$ that your basis can
represent exactly --- a straight line with $p = 1$, say --- the error is zero at every
refinement and you learn nothing at all. Pick something your space genuinely has to work to
approximate.

## Why the estimate describes our solution

Here is the gap Class 17 left open. The a-priori estimate

$$ \|e\|_{H^s(\Omega)} \leq C h^{\beta} \|u\|_{H^{k+1}(\Omega)} $$

comes from **approximation theory**. It says: given a mesh and a polynomial degree, here is
how close the *best possible* function in that space gets to $u$. It is a statement about the
space, and it knows nothing about our solver, our stiffness matrix, or Galerkin's method.

So why are we entitled to use it to describe $u^h$, which is whatever our linear solve
happened to produce? There is no reason to expect those two things to be related --- unless
we prove it. That proof is today's second piece, and it comes in two steps.

### Step one: the error is invisible to the approximation space

Write the left side of the weak form as

$$ a(w, v) := \int_\Omega w_{,x}\, v_{,x} \, dx .$$

This is not new notation for anything new: $a(\cdot,\cdot)$ is exactly what your stiffness
matrix computes, since $K_{AB} = a(N_A, N_B)$.

Now put the two problems side by side. The exact solution satisfies the weak form against
**every** admissible function $w$:

$$ a(u, w) = L(w) \qquad \text{for all } w \in \mathcal{V} ,$$

where $L(w)$ collects the forcing and boundary terms. Our computed solution satisfies the
same equation, but only against the functions we actually built:

$$ a(u^h, w^h) = L(w^h) \qquad \text{for all } w^h \in \mathcal{V}^h .$$

Here is the one observation that makes everything work: **every function in $\mathcal{V}^h$
is also in $\mathcal{V}$.** Our basis functions are legitimate admissible functions; they are
just a small subset of them. So the first equation is true for $w = w^h$ as well, and we may
subtract the second from it:

$$ \boxed{\; a\!\left(u - u^h,\; w^h\right) = 0 \qquad \text{for all } w^h \in \mathcal{V}^h \;}$$

This is **Galerkin orthogonality**. In words: *measured in the energy pairing, the error is
orthogonal to everything our approximation space can represent.* The space cannot see its own
error. If it could, the method would have used that information and done better.

### Step two: so $u^h$ is the best the space can do

Define the **energy norm** by

$$ \|v\|_E := \sqrt{a(v,v)} .$$

For our problem this is just the size of a function's derivative, so it is the $H^1$ part of
the error you have already been computing.

Now take any $w^h$ in the space --- any competitor at all --- and split the difference
between $u$ and it into two pieces:

$$ u - w^h = \underbrace{\left(u - u^h\right)}_{\text{the error}} + \underbrace{\left(u^h - w^h\right)}_{\text{lives in } \mathcal{V}^h} .$$

Measure the size of both sides in the energy norm. Because $a(\cdot,\cdot)$ is symmetric, this
expands the way a squared length does, and the cross term is $a(u - u^h,\, u^h - w^h)$ ---
which is zero, by Galerkin orthogonality, since the second slot lives in $\mathcal{V}^h$.
What is left is

$$ \left\|u - w^h\right\|_E^2 = \left\|u - u^h\right\|_E^2 + \left\|u^h - w^h\right\|_E^2 .$$

That is the Pythagorean theorem, with $a(\cdot,\cdot)$ playing the role of the dot product.
The last term cannot be negative, so dropping it gives

$$ \boxed{\; \left\|u - u^h\right\|_E \;\leq\; \left\|u - w^h\right\|_E \qquad \text{for every } w^h \in \mathcal{V}^h \;}$$

**The finite element solution is the best approximation in its space, measured in the energy
norm.** No other combination of your basis functions gets closer. This result is called
**Céa's lemma**, and it is what licenses Class 17's estimate: a bound on how well the best
polynomial does is automatically a bound on how well *we* do.

It is also the precise version of something this course has been claiming since Class 5 ---
that the finite element method is a **projection**, not an interpolation. It does not pass
through $u$ at the nodes and hope for the best. It finds the closest point in the space,
in exactly the sense that dropping a perpendicular finds the closest point on a plane.

### A reading of this worth carrying forward

Saying $u^h$ is the closest point is the same as saying $u^h$ **minimizes** the error over
everything in the space:

$$ \left\|u - u^h\right\|_E = \min_{w^h \in \mathcal{V}^h} \left\|u - w^h\right\|_E .$$

Keep that word *minimizes* in mind. There are two different minimization statements in this
course and it is worth not confusing them. This one is about the **approximation**: of all
the answers we could have built, we got the closest. The other one, in **Class 23**, is about
the **physics**: the true solution $u$ is the one that minimizes the total potential energy
of the system. The two are related, and Class 23 will also explain where the constant $C$ in
the a-priori estimate comes from.

## When a measured rate is not what you expected

You will run a convergence study and get a number that is not $\beta$. Usually nothing is
wrong. Three ordinary reasons, worth recognizing so you can tell a bug from a non-bug:

**You are not refined enough yet.** The estimate is asymptotic --- it describes behavior as
$h \to 0$. On coarse meshes the measured rate typically creeps up on $\beta$ from below
rather than hitting it. Seeing 1.94 where you expected 2.00 is normal; refine once more and
watch it move.

**You have hit machine precision.** This one surprises people. At high polynomial degree the
error drops so fast that after two or three refinements it reaches roundoff, around
$10^{-16}$, and it cannot get any smaller. The slope then flattens toward zero, and a plot
that was beautifully straight suddenly bends. The method has not stopped working; you have
run out of digits. **HW 12 Problem 3 asks for $p=5$, so you should expect to see this.**

**Your quadrature is not good enough for the error integral.** Class 17 warned about this and
it is worth repeating, because it is the one that actually is your fault. The error
$e = u - u^h$ is not a polynomial, since $u$ generally is not, so the rule that integrates
your stiffness matrix exactly will *not* integrate the error norm exactly. Use more points
than you think you need, and confirm that adding more does not change the answer.

## Where this is going

- **Class 19** moves to multiple dimensions and takes up the surface integrals that Neumann
  conditions require, which have no one-dimensional counterpart. Project 2 is assigned.
- **Class 23** returns to the energy idea from the other side: the minimization form of the
  problem, symmetric positive definiteness, and the question of whether a solution exists
  at all.
